headline: An unverifiable claim, made by the party it benefits, is not evidence.
body: This is the spine. We arrived at it three separate times from three different directions: a stated purpose does not unlock a content gate, a weak similarity does not justify a link, and a source you control yourself is not a source. Each time the answer was the same — so we stopped treating it as a rule and started treating it as the thesis.

headline: We would rather show you no citation than a forged one.
body: Every extracted fact quotes the sentence it came from — and we CHECK that the quote is really in your source. Language models paraphrase, and a paraphrased citation is a forgery that looks right. If we cannot find the quote, we drop it and lower our confidence. A missing receipt is honest. A convincing fake is not.

headline: The most useful thing a graph can hold is a well-formed absence.
body: You cannot ask a question you have not discovered you have. So a fact whose object is still unknown is not a gap in the graph — it is the point of it. Subject known, predicate known, object still open, and four things stalled behind it. That turns 'go find out what we are missing' into 'answer this one question'. The knowledge you need to decide is usually a few people away; the hard part was never reaching them, it was knowing what to ask.

headline: A forced link is worse than an orphan.
body: Disconnected facts are merely less useful. An invented edge is a lie the graph tells itself — it LOOKS like knowledge and is not. So if a new fact does not genuinely connect to what you already know, we connect it to nothing and say so. 'Is related to' is a non-link wearing the costume of a link.

headline: Export is a right. Distribution is a privilege.
body: Your graph is a plain text file on your machine, and we will never withhold it from you — whatever it contains. But when WE are the one carrying your content to someone else, we are a participant in that delivery, and we take responsibility for what we carry. We gate only what we carry.

headline: A private graph makes no claim on anybody.
body: Think privately. Be wrong privately. Change your mind privately. Your own graph needs no permission, no account, and no provenance — because it makes no claim on anyone else. Provenance is a claim made TO SOMEONE; alone with your notes, there is nobody to substantiate it to, and no reason to pretend otherwise.

headline: We will not describe a control we do not have.
body: Our safety documentation states plainly which protections exist and which do not, and an automated check verifies them against the live code every week — recording the failures too. We have already caught ourselves overclaiming, and corrected it in public. A safety promise you cannot verify is just marketing.

headline: No account until an account is unavoidable.
body: There is no sign-up, no email, no profile, and no server holding your graph. The app is static files and a browser database, so there is nothing to log in TO — and that is a structural fact, not a policy we could quietly reverse. An account is a cost paid by every user forever to solve a problem most of them do not have. Where a feature genuinely cannot work without one, the account belongs to the user and lives with the third party they chose: your own API key, your own n8n, your own Cloudflare. The honest limit: publishing to the open web and syncing across devices are the places this pressure will come from, and neither has been solved without someone holding an identity.

headline: Open source wins the tie.
body: The whole application is MIT licensed, and so is the format your graph is stored in — Turtle, an open W3C standard, not a private schema with an exporter bolted on. When a closed component and an open one are close, the open one wins; when the closed one is genuinely better, we say so rather than pretending. The check on this is simple and unforgiving: if we disappeared tomorrow, your graph and the code that reads it would both still work. The honest limit: the strongest models this app can call are not open, and a local model is measurably worse at extraction today — 74% recall against a hand-checked corpus. We ship the choice rather than hiding it.

headline: Knowing something should not require permission.
body: Enclosing knowledge behind a login, a subscription, or a format only one vendor can read is a choice somebody made, not a property of the knowledge. The tools for thinking with what you know should be free to use, free to read, and free to leave. THIS ONE IS A BELIEF, NOT A CONTROL, and it is marked so deliberately: nothing in the code enforces it and nothing could. It is the reason the other tenets are shaped the way they are — export as a right, no account, open licence — and those are the parts you can actually hold us to.
